link.title: Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) for Bioinformatics: A Practical Beginner’s Guide

entry.content:
🧬 Day 104of Daily Bioinformatics from Jojy’s Desk

If you have a Windows laptop, do you need to install Linux before you can start learning bioinformatics?

Not necessarily.

A large part of modern bioinformatics happens in a Linux environment — Bash scripting, Conda environments, command-line tools, HPC clusters, workflow managers. Students who use macOS already have a Unix-like terminal. Windows users have traditionally faced a harder choice: dual-boot, a virtual machine, or connect directly to a remote server.

There is a practical middle ground that is often overlooked: Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). It puts a real Linux environment directly inside Windows, without replacing or partitioning anything. You keep your Windows applications, your file browser, your Office suite — and you get a Bash terminal running Ubuntu alongside them.

This post is the guide I wish existed for every bioinformatics workshop where half the participants have Windows laptops.

What WSL actually is

WSL stands for Windows Subsystem for Linux. It allows you to run a Linux distribution directly on Windows without a traditional virtual machine or dual-boot setup. The current version, WSL 2, runs a real Linux kernel inside a lightweight managed virtual machine. For most practical purposes — Bash, Git, Conda, Python, R, bioinformatics command-line tools — it behaves like a native Linux terminal.

Conceptually, your computer looks like this:

Windows
├── Microsoft Office, browser, Windows apps
├── VS Code
└── WSL 2
    └── Ubuntu
        ├── Bash
        ├── Git
        ├── Python / R
        ├── Conda / Bioconda
        └── Bioinformatics tools

For a learner, this means: you can keep using Windows while learning and practicing Linux.

WSL 1 vs WSL 2

WSL 2 is the relevant version for almost everyone. New distributions installed via wsl --install use WSL 2 by default. WSL 2 uses a real Linux kernel, offers better system-call compatibility, and generally better filesystem performance than WSL 1. Check which version you are running with:

wsl -l -v

Use WSL 2 unless you have a specific reason not to.

Why not just use VirtualBox or dual boot?

All approaches can work. The comparison below is practical, not absolute:

Feature WSL 2 Traditional VM Dual Boot
Real Linux kernel Yes Yes Yes
Keep Windows running Yes Yes No
Windows/Linux file integration Excellent Moderate Limited
Setup difficulty Low Moderate Higher
Good for teaching beginners Excellent Good Lower
Large production analyses Limited by laptop Limited by laptop Limited by laptop

WSL is particularly useful for teaching because students do not need to fundamentally change how they use their computer before their first Bash command. The barrier to entry is a single PowerShell command.

Installation

For modern Windows 10 and Windows 11 systems, installation is a single command. Open PowerShell as Administrator and run:

wsl --install

This installs WSL 2 and Ubuntu by default. Restart your computer when prompted. After restarting, Ubuntu will launch and ask you to create a Linux username and password — these do not need to match your Windows credentials.

To install a different Linux distribution:

# See what is available
wsl --list --online

# Install a specific distribution
wsl --install -d Ubuntu-22.04

For beginners, Ubuntu is the best choice — extensive documentation, the largest community, and broad Bioconda support.

Verify the installation

wsl --status
wsl --version
wsl -l -v

Your first Linux commands

Open Ubuntu from the Start menu. The prompt will look like:

username@computer:~$

Try these immediately:

pwd                    # print working directory
ls                     # list files
mkdir bioinformatics   # create a directory
cd bioinformatics      # move into it
pwd                    # confirm where you are
touch test.txt         # create an empty file
ls -lh                 # list with sizes

Then update Ubuntu — do this on any fresh Linux installation before installing anything:

sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade

When prompted for a password, type your Linux password. Nothing will appear on screen while you type — this is normal Linux behaviour.

The commands worth learning first

These appear repeatedly in every bioinformatics workflow:

# Navigation and files
pwd   ls   cd   mkdir   cp   mv   rm

# Viewing and inspecting data
cat   less   head   tail   wc

# Searching and filtering
grep   find   awk   sed   sort   cut

# Compression and transfer
gzip   tar   wget   curl   ssh   rsync

A student who can use these fluently is ready to follow almost any bioinformatics tutorial and ready to connect to an HPC cluster and feel at home.

RAM and storage: the honest numbers

WSL does not create computational resources. If your laptop has 16 GB RAM, WSL has access to some fraction of 16 GB RAM. The analysis requirements determine whether that is enough.

By default, WSL 2 can use up to 50% of total Windows memory (so 8 GB on a 16 GB machine), with processors defaulting to all logical processors available to Windows. These limits are configurable via a .wslconfig file in your Windows user directory:

[wsl2]
memory=8GB
processors=4
swap=4GB

Do not blindly copy these values — set them based on your computer and workload. The WSL defaults are reasonable for most learning scenarios.

For practical bioinformatics use, here is a realistic RAM guide:

RAM Practical use in WSL
8 GB Linux navigation, Git, Python/R, small exercises
16 GB Recommended starting point for learning bioinformatics tools
32 GB Comfortable for moderate local analyses
64 GB+ More capable, but still not a replacement for HPC

Storage follows the same principle. Learning Bash and running small exercises needs a few GB. A real sequencing project needs hundreds of GB to TB — that lives on the HPC, not your laptop.

An important file storage rule

Your Windows C: drive is accessible from WSL at /mnt/c/. This is convenient, but:

For Linux-heavy bioinformatics work, store files in the Linux filesystem, not under /mnt/c/.

Linux tools reading and writing files across the Windows/Linux boundary can be significantly slower. Use your Linux home directory instead:

mkdir -p ~/projects
cd ~/projects
# run your bioinformatics workflows here

To open your current Linux directory in Windows Explorer (when you need to access files from the Windows side):

explorer.exe .

WSL + VS Code

This combination is especially good for teaching and development. Students get the familiar VS Code interface on Windows while their code and terminal run inside Linux.

Install VS Code on Windows, then install the WSL extension (search “WSL” in the Extensions panel). From any WSL project directory:

code .

VS Code opens connected directly to your Linux environment — full IntelliSense, integrated terminal, file browser, all running in Ubuntu. For students who are not yet comfortable living entirely in a terminal, this is a gentler entry point.

Git, Conda, and bioinformatics tools

Git:

sudo apt install git
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your@email.com"
git --version

Git skills learned in WSL transfer directly to any Linux server or HPC.

Conda (Miniforge recommended):

wget https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
bash Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
# Restart terminal after installation
conda --version

From here, create isolated environments exactly as you would on an HPC:

conda create -n bioinfo -c bioconda fastqc trimmomatic
conda activate bioinfo
fastqc --version

The environment-management concepts are identical to what students will use on a remote Linux server later.

WSL as a stepping stone to HPC

This is the most underappreciated educational value of WSL. A student who learns Linux navigation, Bash scripting, Git, and Conda locally in WSL is prepared to connect to an HPC and not feel completely lost:

Step 1:  Install WSL
Step 2:  Learn Linux navigation (pwd, ls, cd, mkdir)
Step 3:  Learn file manipulation (cp, mv, grep, awk)
Step 4:  Learn Git
Step 5:  Learn Conda environments
Step 6:  Run small bioinformatics tools (FastQC, fastp, samtools)
Step 7:  Write Bash scripts
Step 8:  SSH into HPC — ssh username@hpc.edu
Step 9:  Learn SLURM (sbatch, squeue, sacct)
Step 10: Scale up real analyses

WSL does not need to run your large analysis. It can simply be your local Linux terminal that you use to develop scripts, then SSH into the cluster to run them at scale:

Windows laptop
      ↓
    WSL
      ↓  ssh
    HPC cluster
      ├── SLURM
      ├── Large RAM
      ├── Many CPUs
      └── Large storage

What WSL is good for and where it has limits

WSL works well for:

  • Learning Linux and Bash
  • Learning Git
  • Learning Conda
  • Python and R development
  • Small FASTQ exercises and practice datasets
  • Testing and developing scripts before HPC submission
  • Teaching workshops
  • SSH access to HPC

Think carefully before using WSL for:

  • Large reference databases (Kraken2, GTDB-Tk full databases)
  • Moderate genome or metagenome assembly
  • Docker-heavy workflows
  • Large local datasets

Move to HPC or cloud for:

  • Hundreds of sequencing samples
  • Large metagenomic assemblies
  • High-memory analyses
  • Highly parallel production pipelines
  • Large MAG workflows

The key point: WSL provides the environment. It does not create computational resources. A 16 GB laptop with WSL is still a 16 GB laptop.

Useful WSL management commands

Run these from PowerShell or Command Prompt, not from inside Ubuntu:

wsl --status          # check WSL status
wsl --version         # WSL version
wsl -l -v             # list distributions and versions
wsl --update          # update WSL
wsl --shutdown        # shut down all WSL instances
wsl --list --online   # see available distributions

Quick reference: setup checklist

# 1. Install WSL (PowerShell as Administrator)
wsl --install

# 2. After restarting: update Ubuntu
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

# 3. Install Git
sudo apt install git

# 4. Install Miniforge (Conda)
wget https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
bash Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh

# 5. Install VS Code on Windows, then connect:
code .

# 6. Create your first project directory
mkdir -p ~/projects && cd ~/projects

The honest summary

WSL does not replace Linux HPC. It lowers the barrier to learning it.

For a student with a Windows laptop, asking them to install a second operating system or configure a virtual machine before their first Bash command can turn the first bioinformatics lesson into an IT support session. WSL offers a different path: keep Windows, add Linux, start learning immediately.

The commands learned in WSL — grep, awk, sed, Git, Conda, SSH — are the same commands used on every Linux server and HPC cluster. When a student eventually types ssh username@hpc.edu for the first time, the Linux environment is no longer completely unfamiliar.

That is why WSL has become my first recommendation for Windows users starting out in bioinformatics.

References

  • Microsoft Learn — Install WSL
  • Microsoft Learn — Set up a WSL development environment
  • Microsoft Learn — Comparing WSL 1 and WSL 2
  • Microsoft Learn — Advanced settings configuration in WSL (.wslconfig)
  • Microsoft Learn — WSL basic commands
  • Microsoft Learn — WSL disk space management

Posted as Day 104 of Daily Bioinformatics from Jojy’s Desk. Small steps at the command line open the door to much larger computational workflows.
entry.summary: If you have a Windows laptop and want to learn bioinformatics, you do not need to install a second operating system or configure a virtual machine before your first command. WSL — Windows Subsystem for Linux — puts a real Linux terminal directly on your Windows machine in about ten minutes. This post covers what WSL is, how to install it, RAM and storage realities, VS Code integration, the learning path from Bash to HPC, and the honest limitations: WSL lowers the barrier to learning Linux, but it is not a replacement for an HPC cluster.

Day 6: Specialized Genomic Functions

Estimated Time: 8-12 hours Difficulty: Advanced Prerequisites: Day 5 (Annotation)

📚 Table of Contents

  • Introduction
  • Secondary Metabolites
  • Antimicrobial Resistance
  • Carbohydrate-Active Enzymes
  • Prophages & Viruses
  • CRISPR Systems
  • Mobile Genetic Elements
  • Protein Domains
  • Comparative Analysis
  • Best Practices

🎯 Introduction

Welcome to Day 6! After basic annotation (Day 5), it’s time to discover hidden genomic treasures - specialized functions that make organisms unique.

Today’s discoveries:

  1. 🧪 Secondary metabolites - Antibiotics, toxins, signaling molecules
  2. 💊 Antimicrobial resistance - AMR genes and mechanisms
  3. 🍬 CAZymes - Carbohydrate degradation capabilities
  4. 🦠 Prophages - Integrated viral sequences
  5. ✂️ CRISPR systems - Bacterial immune systems
  6. 🔄 Mobile elements - Transposons, insertion sequences
  7. 🧬 Protein domains - Functional motifs and structures

Why This Matters

Basic annotation tells you:

  • This is a kinase
  • This is a transporter

Specialized analysis reveals:

  • This organism produces penicillin
  • This strain is resistant to carbapenems
  • This microbe can degrade cellulose
  • This genome contains CRISPR-Cas9

🧪 Secondary Metabolites

antiSMASH: Biosynthetic Gene Cluster Detection

antiSMASH (antibiotics & Secondary Metabolite Analysis SHell) is the gold standard for BGC detection.

Installation

# Create environment
conda create -n antismash -c bioconda antismash
conda activate antismash

# Download databases (~15 GB)
download-antismash-databases

Basic Usage

conda activate antismash

# Single genome
antismash \
    --output-dir antismash_output/genome1 \
    --genefinding-tool prodigal \
    --cpus 8 \
    genome1.gbk

# With all features enabled
antismash \
    --output-dir antismash_output/genome1 \
    --genefinding-tool prodigal \
    --knownclusterblast \
    --subclusterblast \
    --clusterblast \
    --smcog-trees \
    --cpus 8 \
    genome1.gbk

Input formats:

  • GenBank (.gbk) - recommended
  • FASTA (.fa) - requires gene finding

antiSMASH Output

antismash_output/genome1/
├── genome1.gbk                    # Annotated genome
├── genome1.json                   # Machine-readable results
├── index.html                     # Interactive visualization
├── regions.js                     # BGC regions
├── knownclusterblast/            # Hits to known BGCs
└── svg/                          # Cluster visualizations

BGC types detected:

  • Polyketides (PKS)
  • Non-ribosomal peptides (NRPS)
  • Terpenes
  • Bacteriocins
  • Siderophores
  • RiPPs (Ribosomally synthesized and Post-translationally modified Peptides)

Parse antiSMASH Results

please use parse_antismash.py from Day 6 →

BiG-SCAPE: BGC Similarity Analysis

BiG-SCAPE compares BGCs across multiple genomes to identify families.

Installation

conda create -n bigscape -c bioconda bigscape
conda activate bigscape

Usage

# Collect all BGC GenBank files from antiSMASH
mkdir bigscape_input
cp antismash_output/*/regions/*.gbk bigscape_input/

# Run BiG-SCAPE
bigscape \
    -i bigscape_input \
    -o bigscape_output \
    --pfam_dir ~/pfam_database \
    --cores 8 \
    --mode auto

# Visualize
firefox bigscape_output/network_files/index.html

BiG-SCAPE output:

  • BGC families (grouped by similarity)
  • Network visualization
  • Comparative analysis across genomes

💊 Antimicrobial Resistance

CARD-RGI: Comprehensive AMR Database

RGI (Resistance Gene Identifier) uses CARD database for AMR detection.

Installation

conda create -n rgi -c bioconda rgi
conda activate rgi

# Download CARD database
rgi load --card_json ~/card_database/card.json

# Verify
rgi database --version

Usage

conda activate rgi

# Predict AMR from proteins
rgi main \
    --input_sequence proteins.faa \
    --input_type protein \
    --output_file rgi_output \
    --clean \
    --num_threads 8

# From nucleotides (slower but more sensitive)
rgi main \
    --input_sequence genome.fa \
    --input_type contig \
    --output_file rgi_output \
    --clean \
    --num_threads 8 \
    --include_loose

RGI output columns:

  • ORF_ID
  • ARO (Antibiotic Resistance Ontology)
  • Drug Class
  • Resistance Mechanism
  • AMR Gene Family

Parse RGI Results

Use parse_rgi.py from Day 6 →

ABRicate: Fast AMR Screening

ABRicate screens multiple AMR databases quickly.

Installation

conda create -n abricate -c bioconda abricate
conda activate abricate

# Update databases
abricate-get_db --db all

Usage

conda activate abricate

# Screen against all databases
abricate genome.fa > abricate_results.tab

# Specific database
abricate --db card genome.fa > card_results.tab
abricate --db resfinder genome.fa > resfinder_results.tab
abricate --db vfdb genome.fa > virulence_results.tab

# Batch processing
abricate genomes/*.fa > all_genomes_amr.tab

# Summary
abricate --summary all_genomes_amr.tab > amr_summary.tab

Available databases:

  • card (CARD)
  • resfinder (ResFinder)
  • ncbi (NCBI AMRFinderPlus)
  • argannot
  • megares
  • vfdb (Virulence factors)
  • plasmidfinder

🍬 Carbohydrate-Active Enzymes (CAZymes)

dbCAN2: CAZyme Annotation

dbCAN identifies enzymes that degrade, modify, or create carbohydrates.

Installation

conda create -n dbcan -c bioconda dbcan
conda activate dbcan

# Download databases
dbcan_build --help

Usage

conda activate dbcan

# Run dbCAN
run_dbcan \
    proteins.faa \
    protein \
    --out_dir dbcan_output \
    --db_dir ~/dbcan_db \
    --tools all \
    --threads 8

# Output: dbcan_output/overview.txt

CAZyme families:

  • GH - Glycoside Hydrolases (breakdown)
  • GT - Glycosyl Transferases (synthesis)
  • PL - Polysaccharide Lyases
  • CE - Carbohydrate Esterases
  • AA - Auxiliary Activities
  • CBM - Carbohydrate-Binding Modules

Parse dbCAN Results

Use parse_dbcan.py from Day 6 →

🦠 Prophages & Viruses

VirSorter2: Viral Sequence Detection

VirSorter2 identifies viral sequences in genomes and metagenomes.

Installation

conda create -n virsorter2 -c bioconda virsorter=2
conda activate virsorter2

# Setup database
virsorter setup -d ~/virsorter2-db -j 4

Usage

conda activate virsorter2

# Run VirSorter2
virsorter run \
    -i genome.fa \
    -w virsorter2_output \
    --min-length 5000 \
    --min-score 0.5 \
    -j 8 \
    all

# High-confidence viral sequences
cat virsorter2_output/final-viral-boundary.tsv

VirSorter2 output:

  • Prophage regions
  • Viral score (0-1)
  • Boundary coordinates
  • Gene content

PHASTER: PHAge Search Tool Enhanced Release

PHASTER identifies prophages with detailed annotation.

Note: PHASTER is primarily a web service.

Web interface: https://phaster.ca/

Alternative: Use VirSorter2 + CheckV

# CheckV for viral genome quality
conda create -n checkv -c bioconda checkv
conda activate checkv

# Download database
checkv download_database ~/checkv-db

# Run CheckV on VirSorter2 results
checkv end_to_end \
    virsorter2_output/final-viral-combined.fa \
    checkv_output \
    -d ~/checkv-db \
    -t 8

✂️ CRISPR Systems

CRISPRCasFinder: Detect CRISPR-Cas Systems

# Installation
conda create -n crisprcasfinder -c bioconda crisprcasfinder
conda activate crisprcasfinder

# Run
CRISPRCasFinder.pl \
    -in genome.fa \
    -out crispr_output \
    -cas \
    -keep

MinCED: Simple CRISPR Detection

conda create -n minced -c bioconda minced
conda activate minced

# Quick CRISPR detection
minced genome.fa crispr_output.txt

# Parse results
grep "CRISPR" crispr_output.txt

CRISPR system types:

  • Type I (most common in bacteria)
  • Type II (Cas9 - CRISPR editing)
  • Type III
  • Type IV-VI (rare)

🔄 Mobile Genetic Elements

ISfinder: Insertion Sequences

# Use ABRicate with custom IS database
abricate --db isfinder genome.fa > is_results.tab

# Or BLAST against ISfinder database
blastn \
    -query genome.fa \
    -db ~/isfinder_db/ISfinder \
    -outfmt 6 \
    -num_threads 8 \
    > is_blast.out

Integron Finder

conda create -n integron_finder -c bioconda integron_finder
conda activate integron_finder

# Find integrons
integron_finder \
    --local-max \
    --cpu 8 \
    genome.fa

Integrons contain:

  • Integration sites
  • Gene cassettes
  • Often AMR genes

🧬 Protein Domains & Functions

InterProScan: Comprehensive Domain Analysis

InterProScan searches multiple protein signature databases.

Installation

# Large download - recommend using web service
# Or install locally:
wget ftp://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/software/unix/iprscan/5/5.XX-XX.X/interproscan-5.XX-XX.X-64-bit.tar.gz
tar -xzf interproscan-5.XX-XX.X-64-bit.tar.gz

Usage

# Run InterProScan
interproscan.sh \
    -i proteins.faa \
    -f TSV,GFF3 \
    -o interproscan_output \
    --cpu 8 \
    --goterms \
    --pathways

Databases searched:

  • Pfam (protein families)
  • PROSITE (patterns)
  • PRINTS
  • SMART
  • TIGRFAMs
  • PANTHER
  • Gene3D
  • Superfamily

Parse InterProScan

Use parse_ipr.py from Day 6 →

📊 Comprehensive Analysis Workflow

Complete Specialized Function Pipeline

Use comprehensive_analysis.sh from Day 6 →

📈 Comparative Analysis

Compare Specialized Functions Across Genomes

Use compare_specialized_functions.py from Day 6 →

💡 Best Practices

Before Analysis

  • ✅ Have complete gene predictions (Prodigal/Prokka)
  • ✅ Use GenBank format for antiSMASH
  • ✅ Check genome quality (comp >80%, cont <5%)
  • ✅ Ensure databases are updated

During Analysis

  • ✅ Run tools in priority order (fast → slow)
  • ✅ Use multiple tools for AMR (RGI + ABRicate)
  • ✅ Save intermediate files
  • ✅ Document tool versions

After Analysis

  • ✅ Validate hits manually (especially AMR)
  • ✅ Check for false positives
  • ✅ Cross-reference with literature
  • ✅ Visualize results

🔧 Troubleshooting

antiSMASH: No BGCs detected

# Check input format
head genome.gbk

# Try with relaxed detection
antismash --minimal ...

# Ensure genome is annotated

RGI: No results

# Update CARD database
rgi load --card_json ~/card_database/card.json

# Try --include_loose for more hits
rgi main --include_loose ...

dbCAN: Low CAZyme count

# Use all three tools
run_dbcan --tools all ...

# Check protein quality
grep ">" proteins.faa | wc -l

📈 Expected Results

Typical Findings per Genome

Feature Typical Range
BGCs 5-30
AMR genes 0-50
CAZymes 50-500
Prophages 0-10
CRISPR arrays 0-5
Integrons 0-5

Visulaizations

📊 1. bgc_heatmap.R - BGC Distribution

What it does:

● Visualizes antiSMASH BGC distributions across genomes ● Creates 3 heatmap variants (basic, custom colors, annotated) ● Includes toy data built-in ● Automatic clustering by BGC similarity

Outputs:

● bgc_heatmap_basic.pdf - Simple clustered heatmap ● bgc_heatmap_custom.pdf - Custom gradient (white → gold → red → purple) ● bgc_heatmap_annotated.pdf - With annotations for BGC richness ● bgc_summary.csv - Summary statistics

Toy data included: 15 genomes × 9 BGC types

🍬 2. cazyme_bubble_plot.R - CAZyme Analysis

What it does:

● Creates bubble plots showing CAZyme family distributions ● Bubble size = CAZyme count ● Color = Genome completion percentage ● Includes heatmap and bar plot variants ● Analyzes degradation capabilities

Outputs:

● cazyme_bubble_plot.pdf - Main bubble visualization ● cazyme_bubble_plot_alt.pdf - Alternative color scheme ● cazyme_total_barplot.pdf - Total counts by taxonomic order ● cazyme_heatmap.pdf - Clustered heatmap ● cazyme_summary.csv - Summary with degradation analysis

Toy data included: 12 taxonomic orders × 6 CAZyme families

All R-codes available in *Day 6 →

Processing Time (8-core laptop)

Tool Single Genome 10 Genomes
antiSMASH 30-60 min 8-10 hrs
RGI 5-10 min 1-2 hrs
ABRicate 1-2 min 15-20 min
dbCAN 10-20 min 2-3 hrs
VirSorter2 20-40 min 5-7 hrs
InterProScan 1-2 hrs 15-20 hrs

✅ Success Checklist

  • BGCs identified and annotated
  • AMR profile generated
  • CAZyme repertoire characterized
  • Prophages detected
  • CRISPR systems identified
  • Mobile elements cataloged
  • Protein domains annotated
  • Comparative analysis completed

📚 Key Resources

Tools & Databases

  • antiSMASH
  • CARD
  • ABRicate
  • dbCAN
  • VirSorter2
  • InterProScan

➡️ What’s Next?

Congratulations! You’ve discovered the specialized capabilities of your genomes!

Next steps:

  • Comparative genomics
  • Pangenome analysis
  • Phylogenomics
  • Publication!
