entry.content:
🧬 Day 5 of 5 — Benchmarking Host-Read Removal for High-Host-Content Metagenomes

This series started with a deceptively simple question: which tool should you use to remove human reads from a host-associated metagenome? Over four days, that question expanded considerably. The benchmark moved from timing comparisons and removal percentages to read-level concordance and the practical question of whether differences in filtering change downstream microbiome profiles. Today I bring all of that together.

The central lesson is one worth stating upfront: host-removal benchmarking should not be reduced to a single percentage column. The percentage of reads removed is necessary information — but it is not sufficient. A tool that removes more reads is not automatically better. A tool that runs faster is not automatically acceptable. The question is whether differences in filtering affect the microbial signal that downstream analyses are intended to measure.

The benchmark dataset

Five anonymized paired-end metagenomes processed after standardized fastp preprocessing. Total input across all samples:

194,488,502 read pairs

Host content varied substantially:

Sample Input read pairs Host content
Sample 1 41,644,670 Very high (~95%)
Sample 2 43,344,280 Very high (~98%)
Sample 3 41,089,173 Moderate (~22%)
Sample 4 31,349,380 Low (~10%)
Sample 5 37,060,999 High (~86%)

This range was deliberate. A host-removal method needs to perform sensibly in both microbe-rich and host-dominated samples. A tool that looks excellent on a low-host sample may behave differently when 95% of the library is human.

Human-read removal rates

Sample BMTagger Bowtie2 BBMap GRCh38 BBMap masked hg19 Cleanifier
Sample 1 94.88% 89.76% 89.85% 85.57% 95.73%
Sample 2 97.91% 94.82% 93.26% 88.44% 98.88%
Sample 3 22.51% 21.72% 21.25% 20.19% 22.72%
Sample 4 10.52% 10.14% 9.83% 9.30% 10.61%
Sample 5 86.07% 83.71% 82.19% 78.71% 86.83%
Mean 62.38% 60.03% 59.28% 56.44% 62.95%

A consistent ranking emerged across all five samples:

Cleanifier ≈ BMTagger
      >
Bowtie2 ≈ BBMap GRCh38
      >
BBMap masked hg19

BBMap with the masked hg19 reference consistently removed fewer reads than BBMap with GRCh38.p12. This comparison illustrates the importance of documenting the exact reference: the two runs differed in both genome assembly and masking, so the observed difference cannot be attributed to masking alone. That was the central methodological lesson of Day 3.

But more removal is not automatically better. The table above does not tell you whether the reads each tool removes are genuinely human. That question required a different kind of analysis.

Computational performance

Tool Mean wall-clock runtime Approximate peak RAM
BMTagger ~73.2 min ~8.0 GB
Bowtie2 ~50.7 min ~4.0 GB
BBMap GRCh38 ~77.3 min ~45.5 GB
BBMap masked hg19 ~55.6 min ~44.3 GB
Cleanifier ~1.56 min ~6.6 GB

Cleanifier was approximately 47× faster than BMTagger while producing nearly identical overall removal rates. For larger cohorts, this runtime difference can substantially reduce aggregate compute time, although total wall-clock completion depends on scheduling, parallelism, and I/O.

BBMap’s RAM requirement (~45 GB) stands out as a practical constraint. On a shared HPC cluster, scheduling 45 GB per job limits how many samples run simultaneously and requires careful resource planning. Cleanifier’s ~6.6 GB footprint is comparatively easy to schedule on typical HPC nodes.

Read-level discordance analysis

Removal percentages describe aggregate behavior. They do not reveal what happens at the level of individual reads. To go deeper, I reconstructed read-pair-level classifications for BMTagger and Cleanifier — the two tools that removed the most reads — across all 194.5 million pairs.

Every read pair was placed into one of four categories:

BMTagger Cleanifier Category
Remove Remove Both remove — concordant removal
Remove Keep BMTagger-only
Keep Remove Cleanifier-only
Keep Keep Neither removes — concordant retention

The result:

Category Read pairs % of total
Both remove 126,193,291 64.88%
BMTagger-only 204,189 0.10%
Cleanifier-only 1,373,154 0.71%
Neither removes 66,717,868 34.31%
Total discordant 1,577,343 0.81%

The two methods agree on 99.19% of all read pairs. That level of concordance is reassuring — the two tools are largely making the same calls. But the disagreement is sharply asymmetric: ~87% of all discordant pairs are Cleanifier-only removals — reads that Cleanifier removes but BMTagger retains. The asymmetry is worth documenting, but disagreement alone does not establish which classification is correct or whether a downstream taxonomic result changes.

Do different filtering decisions change downstream taxonomy?

The discordance analysis identifies where BMTagger and Cleanifier make different decisions. It does not, by itself, tell us whether those differences alter the community profile that a researcher would report. That is why an additional downstream comparison is valuable.

In this benchmark, the retained reads from BMTagger and Cleanifier were taken forward for taxonomic profiling. The downstream taxonomic profiles examined did not show noticeable differences between the two workflows. This observation is important because a small read-level disagreement need not produce a meaningful change in the taxa represented in the final abundance table. It should not, however, be interpreted as proof that every read was classified correctly or that all possible downstream analyses will agree.

A simple illustration using five fictional taxa

The table below is a toy example for explanation only. These are invented taxa labels and invented relative abundances, not measurements from the benchmark or an export of the taxonomy results. It shows what near-identical downstream profiles can look like even when the upstream host-removal tools do not classify every read pair identically.

Illustrative taxon BMTagger workflow Cleanifier workflow
Taxon 1 40.0% 40.1%
Taxon 2 30.0% 29.9%
Taxon 3 15.0% 15.0%
Taxon 4 10.0% 10.0%
Taxon 5 5.0% 5.0%
Total 100.0% 100.0%

Illustrative values only; do not cite this table as empirical benchmark data.

The useful comparison is not merely the number of reads retained. It is whether the major taxa, their relative abundances, and the biological interpretation remain stable after the filtering step. In the profiles examined here, the downstream results were similar despite differences in read-level decisions.

For a formal publication, this comparison could be expanded with paired taxon-abundance plots, rank correlations, compositional distances, and sample-level concordance. Those additional quantitative results are not presented here; the observation above is deliberately limited to the downstream profiles that were examined.

Beyond host-read removal: what else can Cleanifier do?

The five-sample benchmark above evaluated human DNA read filtering. While preparing the final comparison, I also looked more closely at what Cleanifier can do outside that specific use case. Its underlying idea is general: compare sequencing reads with a reference index built from sequences that we want to identify or exclude. The biological interpretation depends entirely on the index being used.

Cleanifier uses spaced-seed (gapped k-mer) matching rather than conventional base-by-base alignment. Its published implementation supports paired-end and single-end FASTQ, compressed reads, a fast sampling mode, a more sensitive mode, and custom indexes. These are documented software capabilities, not additional experiments performed in this benchmark.

1. Count likely host reads before deciding to remove them

Not every analysis needs to begin by immediately writing a new host-depleted FASTQ. Sometimes the first question is simply: How much of this sequencing library appears to be host-derived?

Cleanifier includes a --count option that performs classification without writing filtered read files. This can be useful for an initial survey of a sequencing batch, for comparing the host-read burden across samples, or for prioritizing samples that might need deeper sequencing. The exact statistics printed by a particular release should be checked with its --help output and captured in the run log.

# Example: classify/count against a human index, without writing filtered FASTQ
cleanifier filter \
  --index /path/to/human_index \
  --fastq sample_R1.fastq.gz \
  --pairs sample_R2.fastq.gz \
  --prefix sample_host_screen \
  --count 2>&1 | tee sample_host_screen.log

This produces an index-based estimate of the host-associated fraction, not an independent ground-truth measurement of host DNA. A count-only screening result can help plan a project, but it should not replace host filtering when the downstream data-sharing or analysis workflow requires decontaminated reads.

2. Explore how much sequencing effort is going into host DNA

Host-read counts can inform quality control and study design. For example, a host-dominated library may contain tens of millions of sequenced pairs but comparatively few reads available for microbial profiling. Across a cohort, a simple table of input pairs, pairs flagged as host, and pairs retained can help identify samples where sequencing depth or extraction efficiency deserves attention.

Illustrative sample Input pairs Pairs flagged as host Estimated host fraction Pairs not flagged
Example A 10,000,000 9,000,000 90% 1,000,000
Example B 10,000,000 5,000,000 50% 5,000,000
Example C 10,000,000 1,000,000 10% 9,000,000

Hypothetical numbers for teaching only; not outputs from the five-sample benchmark.

This is especially useful when comparing libraries with very different host backgrounds. However, read fractions are not cell fractions or microbial biomass measurements: genome sizes, extraction efficiency, amplification, and sequencing biases affect those relationships. Where absolute microbial load is important, complementary measurements such as qPCR may be necessary.

3. Remove ribosomal RNA from metatranscriptomic data

A particularly interesting extension is rRNA depletion for metatranscriptomics. Cleanifier’s project documentation provides a downloadable ribosomal reference index:

# Download the documented rRNA index (requires Cleanifier and an existing directory)
mkdir -p cleanifier_rrna_index
cleanifier download --version ribosomal --checksum --dir cleanifier_rrna_index

In a microbial metatranscriptomics workflow, rRNA can dominate the sequencing output even after laboratory depletion. A computational rRNA-filtering step can enrich the reads available for downstream mRNA-focused functional and expression analyses. Importantly, the rRNA index is different from the human pangenome index: using a human index does not automatically remove rRNA, and rRNA filtering does not by itself remove human DNA or human mRNA.

A conceptual workflow is:

Metatranscriptomic FASTQ
        |
        v
Read quality control / adapter trimming
        |
        v
Screen or filter unwanted host sequences
        |
        v
Screen or filter rRNA using an rRNA reference index
        |
        v
Retained non-rRNA reads for microbial transcript profiling
        |
        v
Gene / pathway expression analysis

The order of host and rRNA screening may vary with the project. For RNA studies, one should also consider host mRNA: a human-sequence index containing cDNA-related content may help flag host-derived transcripts, but this is not equivalent to a validated, comprehensive host-transcript depletion pipeline. The appropriate reference, strandedness, sample type, and sensitivity must be evaluated separately. We did not benchmark host mRNA removal or rRNA depletion in the five DNA metagenomes presented here.

4. Build a custom index for another unwanted sequence class

The underlying Cleanifier method is not restricted to the provided human index. Its documentation describes building custom indexes. Depending on the scientific objective, a researcher could explore an index of known unwanted sequences, such as a particular host reference, technical contaminants, or a defined reference collection.

This is a potential application requiring validation, not a claim that Cleanifier automatically identifies every contaminant. A custom reference will only recognize sequences represented by the index and sufficiently similar to them under the chosen settings. A poorly chosen reference can remove legitimate biological reads.

5. Tune the sensitivity–retention tradeoff

The default --threshold 0.5 controls how much of a read is covered by index-matching spaced seeds before it is filtered; it is not a 50% probability that the read is human. A lower threshold may increase removal sensitivity at the cost of retaining fewer non-target reads. A higher threshold may be more conservative. The --sensitive option checks all eligible spaced seeds rather than the default sampled subset.

# Example of the more sensitive matching mode
cleanifier filter \
  --index /path/to/human_index \
  --fastq sample_R1.fastq.gz \
  --pairs sample_R2.fastq.gz \
  --prefix sample_sensitive \
  --threshold 0.5 \
  --sensitive

These settings can be worth testing on representative samples, especially when the research question involves low-abundance taxa. The reported 47× speed advantage comes from the benchmarked configuration; it should not be assumed for other thresholds, modes, indexes, or RNA workflows.

6. Plan scalable screening on shared computing infrastructure

Cleanifier’s documentation also describes loading an index into shared memory for reuse by multiple processes. In an HPC setting, avoiding repeated loading of a large index may improve throughput when many samples are processed on the same node. Actual gains depend on filesystem behavior, node memory, process concurrency, and how jobs are scheduled.

This suggests a practical separation of tasks: count first for a quick batch-level QC overview, filter when clean FASTQ files are required, and choose a reference index appropriate to the biological material. It also makes sense to keep an auditable per-sample record of the index version, parameters, input counts, retained counts, and runtime.

What was tested here, and what remains an application idea?

Cleanifier application Status in this post
Human-read removal from paired-end DNA metagenomes Benchmarked on five samples
Read-pair agreement with BMTagger Measured across ~194.5 million pairs
Downstream taxonomic comparison Examined for BMTagger vs Cleanifier
Count-only screening (--count) Documented capability; example only
rRNA filtering for metatranscriptomics Documented index; not tested here
Host mRNA screening in RNA data Possible application to validate; not tested here
Custom host or contaminant indexes Documented capability; not tested here
Sensitive mode / threshold tuning Documented options; not benchmarked here

Further reading: Cleanifier documentation, Cleanifier on PyPI, and the Cleanifier methods paper.

Integrated comparison

Dimension BMTagger Bowtie2 BBMap GRCh38 BBMap masked hg19 Cleanifier
Host removal rate Very high High High More conservative Very high
Runtime Slow Moderate Slow Moderate Extremely fast
Peak RAM Moderate Low Very high Very high Moderate
Workflow complexity High (requires decompressed input, post-processing) Low Moderate Moderate Low
Reference strategy GRCh38.p12 GRCh38.p12 GRCh38.p12 Repeat-masked hg19 T2T + pangenome probabilistic
Downstream taxonomy comparison Similar to Cleanifier in profiles examined Not assessed here Not assessed here Not assessed here Similar to BMTagger in profiles examined
Scalability at 100+ samples Limited by runtime Feasible Limited by RAM Limited by RAM Highly practical

A practical decision framework

Before choosing a host-removal tool, ask five questions:

1. Sensitivity — how much residual human sequence is acceptable? The percentage of reads removed is a useful starting point, but it is not a direct measurement of human-read sensitivity without an independent truth set. In high-host samples, percentage-point differences can represent many read pairs, so downstream requirements and residual-host validation should guide acceptable thresholds.

2. Biological preservation — do filtering differences change the microbiome result? Compare downstream taxonomic profiles on the same samples after each host-removal workflow. Similar profiles can be reassuring, but they are not a substitute for independent sensitivity or specificity validation. A benchmark on one sample type may not generalize to another.

3. Compute cost — what is feasible at your intended scale? If you are processing 10 samples, BBMap’s 45 GB RAM requirement is an inconvenience. If you are processing 500 samples with limited cluster allocation, it may be a genuine barrier. Cleanifier’s throughput advantage becomes increasingly important as cohort size grows.

4. Reproducibility — can the exact method be documented? A complete host-removal description includes: tool name and version, reference genome identity, whether the reference was masked, key alignment or filtering parameters, and how paired-end reads were handled. Report the retained-read definition and any downstream comparison used to evaluate biological consistency. “We used Bowtie2” is not a reproducible methods statement.

5. Workflow integration — how does it fit into your pipeline? BMTagger requires decompressed input and produces read-ID lists rather than FASTQ output — extra steps that compound across many samples. Bowtie2 and Cleanifier write paired gzipped FASTQ directly in a single command. At cohort scale, operational simplicity is not a cosmetic concern.

The lesson the benchmark taught

I started this series expecting to produce a table showing which tool removes the most human reads most quickly. What I produced instead was a multi-layered analysis that revealed something more nuanced.

Cleanifier’s ~47× runtime advantage was striking, but the follow-up comparison was equally important: the tools differed on 0.81% of read pairs, yet the downstream taxonomic profiles examined did not show noticeable differences. This puts the computational advantage in biological context without claiming that the tools are identical in every respect.

The benchmark evolved from:

Which tool removes the most human reads?

into:

Do the reads on which tools disagree
change the downstream biological interpretation?

That second question is why benchmarking should extend beyond software timing. Removal percentage and runtime are the starting points; downstream biological consistency adds a crucial layer of evidence.

If you work with host-associated metagenomes, the strongest recommendation from this series is to benchmark host-removal methods on your own sample type before committing to a production workflow. Generic benchmarks are useful starting points, and downstream consistency should be checked for the biological questions that matter in each study.

Sample identifiers remain anonymized throughout this series. All timing measurements were made using /usr/bin/time -v on an HPC cluster with standardized fastp-preprocessed inputs.
entry.summary: The final post in a 5-day series benchmarking BMTagger, Bowtie2, BBMap (GRCh38 and masked hg19), and Cleanifier for human read removal from high-host-content metagenomes. Today brings the integrated comparison: removal rates, runtime, RAM, read-level agreement across 194 million read pairs, a downstream taxonomy comparison, additional Cleanifier capabilities (including count-only screening and rRNA filtering), and a practical decision framework. The key lesson is that filtering performance must be evaluated alongside biological results.

entry.title: Cleanifier: Fast Human Read Removal and the False-Positive Question — Day 4 of 5

link.title: Cleanifier: Fast Human Read Removal and the False-Positive Question — Day 4 of 5

entry.content:
🧬 Day 4 of 5 — Benchmarking Host-Read Removal for High-Host-Content Metagenomes

The first three days of this benchmark established a clear pattern: BMTagger removed the most reads, Bowtie2 was faster and operationally simpler, and BBMap’s output shifted meaningfully depending on which human reference it used. Runtimes ranged from 50 to 77 minutes per sample. Memory requirements peaked at 45 GB for BBMap.

Then I ran Cleanifier. The runtime for Sample 1 — a 41 million read-pair library — came back at 1 minute and 34 seconds.

That number changed the conversation.

A tool that runs in 1.5 minutes while removing roughly the same percentage of reads as a tool that takes 73 minutes is not a minor improvement. It changes what is computationally feasible at scale. But it also raises an important question that a runtime table cannot answer: if Cleanifier removes slightly more reads than the alignment-based tools, and does so much faster, are those extra removed reads actually human — or are some of them microbial?

This post documents the read-level analysis I ran to answer that question.

What Cleanifier is

Cleanifier takes a fundamentally different approach from the alignment tools tested on Days 2 and 3. Rather than aligning reads to a single linear human reference genome, it uses a probabilistic index built from multiple human sequence sources:

  • T2T (Telomere-to-Telomere) complete assembly
  • Human pangenome sequences
  • HLA and variant sequences
  • cDNA-related content

This broader representation of human genomic diversity is why Cleanifier can be both faster and potentially more sensitive than a single-reference aligner — it classifies reads probabilistically against a richer picture of human sequence space rather than performing base-by-base alignment against one reference.

Running Cleanifier

The command is clean and straightforward:

/usr/bin/time -v -o ${SAMPLE}_cleanifier.time.txt \
  cleanifier filter \
    --index human_probabilistic_index \
    --fastq  ${SAMPLE}_R1.fastp.fastq.gz \
    --pairs  ${SAMPLE}_R2.fastp.fastq.gz \
    --prefix ${OUTDIR}/${SAMPLE} \
    --threshold 0.5 \
    --compression gz \
    --compression-threads 16

Key parameters:

Parameter Value What it does
--index Probabilistic human index The pre-built multi-source human index
--threshold 0.5 Classification cutoff Reads with probability ≥ 0.5 of being human are removed
--compression gz Output format Writes gzipped FASTQ directly
--compression-threads 16 Parallel compression Compresses output while classifying — contributes to the runtime advantage

The --threshold value is worth noting. Lowering it (e.g., 0.3) would remove more reads but increase false-positive risk. Raising it (e.g., 0.7) would be more conservative. For this benchmark, 0.5 was used as the default.

Removal percentages: Cleanifier vs BMTagger

Across the five benchmark samples:

Sample BMTagger Cleanifier Difference
Sample 1 94.88% 95.73% +0.85%
Sample 2 97.91% 98.88% +0.97%
Sample 3 22.51% 22.72% +0.21%
Sample 4 10.52% 10.61% +0.09%
Sample 5 86.07% 86.83% +0.76%
Mean 62.38% 62.95% +0.57%

Cleanifier removed slightly more reads than BMTagger in every sample. The difference is largest in the high-host samples (Samples 1, 2, and 5) and negligible in the low-host sample (Sample 4) — a pattern consistent with what was seen when comparing BBMap references on Day 3.

The runtime comparison

Tool Mean wall-clock runtime Approximate peak RAM
BMTagger ~73.2 min ~8.0 GB
Bowtie2 ~50.7 min ~4.0 GB
BBMap GRCh38 ~77.3 min ~45.5 GB
BBMap masked hg19 ~55.6 min ~44.3 GB
Cleanifier ~1.56 min ~6.6 GB

The ~47× runtime advantage over BMTagger is real and reproducible across all five samples. At scale — 100 samples, 200 samples — this is the difference between a preprocessing step that takes a day of cluster time and one that takes under an hour.

The memory requirement (~6.6 GB) is also well within the range of most HPC node configurations, making Cleanifier far easier to schedule than BBMap at scale.

At this point, the obvious summary would be:

“Cleanifier removes at least as many human reads as BMTagger while running 47× faster — it is the clear winner.”

But that conclusion skips the question that matters most for downstream biology: are those extra removed reads genuinely human, or does the probabilistic classification approach introduce microbial false positives?

Read-level discordance analysis

To answer this, I reconstructed read-pair-level classifications for BMTagger and Cleanifier across all five samples. Every original fastp-preprocessed read pair was assigned to one of four categories:

BMTagger decision Cleanifier decision Category
Remove Remove Both remove — high confidence human
Remove Keep BMTagger-only — BMTagger removes, Cleanifier retains
Keep Remove Cleanifier-only — Cleanifier removes, BMTagger retains
Keep Keep Neither removes — retained by both

Across approximately 194.5 million total read pairs:

Category Read pairs
Both remove 126,193,291
BMTagger-only 204,189
Cleanifier-only 1,373,154
Neither removes 66,717,868
Total discordant 1,577,343

Overall disagreement: 1,577,343 / 194,488,502 ≈ 0.81%

The two methods agree on more than 99% of read pairs. But the disagreement is strikingly asymmetric: approximately 87% of all discordant pairs are Cleanifier-only removals — reads that Cleanifier removes but BMTagger retains.

The 1.37 million Cleanifier-only read pairs are the population that demands scrutiny.

What are the Cleanifier-only reads?

The 1,373,154 Cleanifier-only read pairs correspond to 2,746,308 individual sequences. These were extracted and screened against core_nt to ask: do any of these reads have credible microbial matches?

The initial screen identified 79,202 sequences with candidate prokaryotic evidence — about 2.9% of the Cleanifier-only pool.

That initial hit rate sounds concerning. But accepting the top bacterial hit would be too permissive. Human and microbial sequences can produce ambiguous matches for short alignments, conserved regions, low-complexity sequence, and regions where the reference database itself contains contamination. A credible false-positive claim requires competing evidence — the same read must produce stronger evidence for a microbial origin than for a eukaryotic one.

After evaluating bacterial-candidate reads against competing prokaryotic and eukaryotic evidence:

Classification Sequences % of candidates
Confident bacterial 4,319 5.45%
Eukaryotic supported 59,536 75.17%
Ambiguous 13,209 16.68%
Prokaryotic short/weak 2,138 2.70%
Total 79,202 100%

Three quarters of initial bacterial-looking candidates had better eukaryotic support when competing evidence was considered. That is reassuring — it suggests the initial hits were largely due to conserved or repetitive regions with eukaryotic origins, not genuine microbial contamination of the removed pool.

The 4,319 confident bacterial sequences represent the true false-positive concern.

How large is the confirmed bacterial fraction?

Relative to all Cleanifier-only individual sequences:

4,319 / 2,746,308 ≈ 0.157%

Numerically, this is very small. Cleanifier is not indiscriminately removing large numbers of microbial reads.

However — and this matters — the biologically important question is not only about percentages. It is about which organisms those reads come from, and whether their removal affects downstream community interpretation.

Among the confirmed bacterial sequences, several reads matched organisms relevant to host-associated microbial communities, including organisms in genera that can be biologically important in the sample type being studied. The strongest single-organism signal within the confirmed bacterial set came from one taxon in particular — appearing across multiple benchmark samples.

931 confirmed sequences mapped to this organism across three samples. As an absolute number, that is tiny relative to 194 million total read pairs. But if this organism is a biologically important community member in your study system — one that you are specifically trying to quantify or compare between groups — its systematic underrepresentation is not a rounding error. It is a bias that compounds across samples.

The reciprocal control: BMTagger-only reads

At this point it would be tempting to declare Cleanifier the tool with the specificity problem and BMTagger the cleaner baseline. But this comparison only holds if BMTagger’s exclusive removals are genuinely human.

BMTagger exclusively removed 204,189 read pairs — reads that Cleanifier retains but BMTagger discards. These 408,378 individual sequences require the same screening framework:

  • How many produce confident bacterial hits?
  • How many have better eukaryotic support?
  • Are any of them from biologically important host-associated organisms?

The reciprocal control is essential before any specificity claim can be made. If BMTagger-only reads also contain a small confirmed microbial population — even a smaller one — then both tools have measurable false-positive rates, and the comparison shifts from “which tool is specific?” to “which tool has an acceptable false-positive rate given its other advantages?”

That analysis is the last piece of the benchmark, and it forms the core of tomorrow’s Day 5 summary.

What Day 4 established

Cleanifier’s runtime advantage is genuine and large. At ~47× faster than BMTagger with comparable removal rates and a memory footprint that fits comfortably on standard HPC nodes, it changes what is feasible for preprocessing large cohorts.

The false-positive analysis reveals something more nuanced than a simple pass/fail verdict. The vast majority of Cleanifier-only reads have eukaryotic support or are ambiguous — not microbial. A small but confirmed bacterial population does exist among Cleanifier’s exclusive removals. Whether that population represents an acceptable tradeoff depends on the study system, the organisms of interest, and the sequencing depth available.

The honest framing is:

A ~0.16% confirmed bacterial signal among Cleanifier-exclusive removals may be negligible for most applications — but it is not zero, and it is not evenly distributed across all organisms.

That distinction is what the Day 5 comparison table will need to make explicit.

What comes tomorrow

Day 5 brings the complete comparison: all five methods side by side, with removal rates, runtime, RAM, read-level agreement, the reciprocal BMTagger-only screen, and a practical recommendation for researchers working with high-host-content metagenomes.

The final question is not “which tool removed the highest percentage?” It is which tool gives the best practical balance across all the dimensions that actually matter for reproducible, biologically interpretable research.
entry.summary: Day 4 of the host-read removal benchmark. Cleanifier finished each sample in under two minutes — roughly 47 times faster than BMTagger — while removing a nearly identical percentage of reads. But a faster tool that removes more reads raises an important question: are those extra removed reads actually human? This post documents a read-level discordance analysis comparing Cleanifier and BMTagger on approximately 194 million read pairs, screening the reads each tool removes exclusively against a nucleotide database to ask whether any confirmed microbial signal is present among them.

entry.title: BBMap and the Human Reference Problem: Why Your Database Choice Matters as Much as Your Tool — Day 3 of 5

link.title: BBMap and the Human Reference Problem: Why Your Database Choice Matters as Much as Your Tool — Day 3 of 5

entry.content:
🧬 Day 3 of 5 — Benchmarking Host-Read Removal for High-Host-Content Metagenomes Day 1 framed the benchmark. Day 2 showed that two well-known alignment tools — BMTagger and Bowtie2 — produce noticeably different removal rates even when both use GRCh38 as the reference. The natural next question was: how much of that difference is the algorithm, and how much is the reference?

Today’s post answers that directly. I ran BBMap twice — same samples, same mapping parameters, same tool — against two different human references: the standard GRCh38.p12 and a repeat-masked hg19. The only thing that changed between the two runs was the database.

The result was a 3–5 percentage point difference in host removal across the high-host samples.

This is the most important lesson in the entire benchmark series: the reference is part of the method. Writing “human reads were removed with BBMap” in a Methods section is not a complete description. Stating the reference genome, the masking strategy, and the key alignment parameters is what makes a host-removal workflow reproducible.

What BBMap is and why it is used here

BBMap is a splice-aware short- and long-read aligner developed at the Joint Genome Institute. For host removal it offers a useful combination: a k-mer-seeded hybrid mapping strategy that is highly sensitive, configurable alignment thresholds that let you tune the sensitivity/specificity balance, and output flags that directly separate unmapped (retained microbial) reads from mapped (human) reads in a single command.

The key output flags are:

  • outu1 / outu2 — reads that did not map to the human reference → your retained microbial reads
  • outm1 / outm2 — reads that did map → your discarded human reads

This direct separation in a single pass is operationally cleaner than tools that require a post-processing extraction step.

The benchmark design for Day 3

The same fastp-preprocessed paired-end reads used on Days 1 and 2 were passed to BBMap twice, with only the path= argument changed between runs:

Run Reference All other parameters
BBMap GRCh38 GRCh38.p12 (standard) Identical
BBMap masked hg19 Repeat-masked hg19 Identical

This is the controlled comparison that isolates the reference effect from the algorithm effect. When the only variable between two runs is the database, any difference in output is a reference effect.

BBMap: full command

Both runs used these parameters:

/usr/bin/time -v -o ${SAMPLE}_bbmap_${REF_NAME}.time.txt \
  bbmap.sh \
    minid=0.95 \
    maxindel=3 \
    bwr=0.16 \
    bw=12 \
    quickmatch \
    fast \
    minhits=2 \
    qtrim=rl \
    trimq=10 \
    untrim \
    path=${REF_DIR} \
    in1=${SAMPLE}_R1.fastp.fastq.gz \
    in2=${SAMPLE}_R2.fastp.fastq.gz \
    outu1=${OUTDIR}/${SAMPLE}_nonhuman_R1.fastq.gz \
    outu2=${OUTDIR}/${SAMPLE}_nonhuman_R2.fastq.gz \
    outm1=${OUTDIR}/${SAMPLE}_human_R1.fastq.gz \
    outm2=${OUTDIR}/${SAMPLE}_human_R2.fastq.gz \
    threads=16 \
    -Xmx48g

Key parameters explained:

Parameter Value What it does
minid=0.95 95% identity threshold Only classify a read as human if ≥95% identity to the reference — reduces false positives
maxindel=3 Max 3 indels Appropriate for short reads; reduces misalignments
bwr=0.16 Bandwidth ratio Controls alignment band width; affects sensitivity/speed tradeoff
quickmatch — Uses faster approximate matching before full alignment
fast — Increases speed at slight sensitivity cost
minhits=2 Min 2 k-mer hits A read must share at least 2 k-mer seeds with the reference before full alignment — reduces spurious mappings
qtrim=rl trimq=10 Quality trim both ends Trim low-quality bases before alignment
untrim — Restore original read length in output after alignment
-Xmx48g 48 GB heap Critical — BBMap loads the reference into memory; undersizing this causes crashes

The -Xmx48g flag deserves attention. BBMap stores the reference index in Java heap memory. For a full human genome reference, this requires tens of gigabytes. If you run BBMap without setting this appropriately for your reference size, it will fail mid-run with an out-of-memory error — sometimes after hours of processing. Always set this flag explicitly and allocate enough memory in your SLURM job request.

Building the BBMap reference database

For GRCh38:

bbmap.sh ref=GRCh38.p12.fa path=GRCh38_BBMap_DB -Xmx48g

For masked hg19:

bbmap.sh ref=hg19_masked.fa path=masked_hg19_DB -Xmx48g

The path= directory stores the pre-built index. Building the index from a full human genome takes 30–60 minutes and substantial memory, but it only needs to be done once. Store the index in a shared project location so all samples use the same database.

What masking actually does

Before looking at the results, it is worth understanding what a masked reference is and why someone would use one.

The human genome contains large amounts of:

  • Repetitive sequence — transposable elements, satellite repeats, tandem repeats
  • Low-complexity regions — homopolymers, simple sequence repeats
  • Conserved sequence — regions similar to genes found in bacteria, archaea, or other eukaryotes

When a short read maps to one of these regions, the alignment may be ambiguous: the read matches the human reference, but it might equally match a microbial sequence. An aggressive mapper will classify it as human and remove it. A more conservative approach would leave it unclassified.

A repeat-masked reference replaces these problematic regions with N characters before indexing. A read that would have mapped to a repetitive or low-complexity human region can no longer map — because that region has been masked out. The mapper therefore retains reads it would otherwise have classified as human.

The trade-off is explicit:

Standard reference (GRCh38):
  Higher sensitivity for human reads
  Risk: some ambiguous/microbial reads classified as human

Masked reference:
  Lower sensitivity for human reads in repetitive regions
  Benefit: reduced false-positive removal of microbial reads

Neither is universally correct. The right choice depends on what matters most for your biological question.

Benchmark results

Across the five samples:

Sample BBMap GRCh38 BBMap masked hg19 Difference
Sample 1 89.85% 85.57% −4.28%
Sample 2 93.26% 88.44% −4.82%
Sample 3 21.25% 20.19% −1.06%
Sample 4 9.83% 9.30% −0.53%
Sample 5 82.19% 78.71% −3.48%
Mean 59.28% 56.44% −2.84%

The masked reference consistently removed fewer reads. The difference is largest in high-host samples (Samples 1, 2, and 5) and smallest in the low-host sample (Sample 4) — which makes intuitive sense. In high-host samples, a larger fraction of reads are genuinely human, so the effect of masking out repetitive regions is proportionally larger.

The tempting but wrong conclusion

Looking at this table, a natural reaction is:

“GRCh38 removes more reads, so it is better.”

This is the wrong conclusion — or at least, it is an incomplete one. The additional reads removed by GRCh38 could represent:

  1. True human reads that the masked reference missed — in which case GRCh38 is more sensitive and the additional removals are correct
  2. Ambiguous reads that map to repetitive regions shared between human and microbial genomes — in which case both references are removing something real, but the GRCh38 run is removing more of the microbial co-mapping reads
  3. Microbial false positives — reads from vaginal community members that share short regions of sequence similarity with unmasked repetitive elements

The removal percentage alone cannot distinguish between these three possibilities. That requires the read-level discordance analysis coming on Day 5, where I map discordant reads back to taxonomic databases and ask what organisms they actually come from.

Computational performance

Approximate mean performance across all five samples:

Configuration Mean wall-clock runtime Approximate peak RAM
BBMap GRCh38 ~77 minutes ~45.5 GB
BBMap masked hg19 ~56 minutes ~44.3 GB

Two things stand out here.

First, BBMap required substantially more RAM than any other tool in this benchmark. BMTagger used ~8 GB, Bowtie2 used ~4 GB, and BBMap needed ~45 GB. This is the most practically significant limitation of BBMap for host removal: on a shared HPC cluster, allocating 45–50 GB per sample limits how many simultaneous jobs you can run on a given node. At scale — 100 samples — this becomes a scheduling bottleneck.

Second, the masked reference was ~27% faster than GRCh38. Since the masked reference has fewer indexable positions (the N-masked regions are ignored), the mapper processes fewer potential alignment targets per read. Faster runtime with lower sensitivity in repetitive regions — a consistent package.

Why the reference is part of the method

This benchmark illustrates a principle that applies well beyond host removal:

The output of a bioinformatics tool is a joint product of the algorithm, the database, the parameters, and the preprocessing. Naming only the tool is an incomplete description.

For host removal specifically, a reproducible Methods section should include:

✓ Tool name and version
✓ Human reference genome (GRCh38, hg19, T2T, etc.)
✓ Whether the reference was masked, and how
✓ Key alignment parameters (identity threshold, minhits, etc.)
✓ How paired-end reads were handled
✓ How unmapped reads were retained

A Methods section that says only “Human reads were removed using BBMap” does not contain enough information for another researcher to reproduce the analysis — or to understand why their results differ if they attempt to.

A complete description would read more like:

Human reads were removed using BBMap (v39.x) mapped against GRCh38.p12, requiring ≥95% nucleotide identity (minid=0.95) and a minimum of 2 k-mer seed hits (minhits=2). Unmapped read pairs were retained for downstream analysis.

That is a reproducible methods statement.

A framework for thinking about host removal

The benchmark has now tested four configurations across three tools. A useful way to organize them:

Host-removal result =
    f(algorithm, reference, parameters, preprocessing)

To isolate algorithm effects:
    → keep reference and parameters constant, vary the tool

To isolate reference effects:
    → keep algorithm and parameters constant, vary the database
      (this is what Day 3 tested)

To evaluate end-to-end performance:
    → use each tool's recommended reference and parameters,
      compare realistic production configurations

All three comparisons answer different questions. A benchmark that only runs each tool with its default settings on a single reference is measuring something, but it is conflating algorithm, reference, and parameter effects in a way that makes it hard to interpret differences.

What comes tomorrow

Day 4 introduces Cleanifier — the newest method in this benchmark and the one that most changed my thinking about the tradeoffs involved.

In the benchmark, Cleanifier produced host-removal percentages close to BMTagger while running in approximately 1.5 minutes per sample. That is not a typo. Where BBMap takes 77 minutes and requires 45 GB of RAM, Cleanifier finished the same sample in under two minutes.

That result was interesting enough that I did not stop at the runtime table. I asked the more important question: what exactly are the reads that Cleanifier removes that the alignment-based tools miss — and vice versa? That read-level investigation became the most analytically interesting part of the benchmark, and it is the focus of Day 4.

Previous posts: Day 1 — Benchmark design and why host removal matters Day 2 — BMTagger vs Bowtie2.
entry.summary: Day 3 of the host-read removal benchmark series. Today's lesson is one most bioinformatics tutorials skip: host-removal performance is determined not only by the algorithm but also by the human reference you map against. I ran BBMap twice — once against GRCh38.p12 and once against a repeat-masked hg19 reference — using identical mapping parameters. The same tool, the same sample, the same settings, a different database: removal rates shifted by 3–5 percentage points. This post explains why that happens, what masking actually does, and why your Methods section should always name the reference, not just the tool.

entry.title: BMTagger vs Bowtie2 for Human Read Removal — Day 2 of 5

link.title: BMTagger vs Bowtie2 for Human Read Removal — Day 2 of 5

entry.content:
🧬 Day 2 of 5 — Benchmarking Host-Read Removal for High-Host-Content Metagenomes

Yesterday I introduced the core challenge of host-read removal: the goal is not simply to remove as many human reads as possible, but to do so without discarding genuine microbial reads from the organisms you actually care about. In host associated metagenomics, where community composition can hinge on the relative abundance of a small number of taxa, that distinction is not academic — it determines whether your downstream biology is real or an artifact.

Today I am working through the first two methods in the benchmark: BMTagger and Bowtie2. Both are alignment-oriented approaches to host removal, both used GRCh38 as the human reference, and both support paired-end reads. But they differ substantially in workflow complexity, computational requirements, and how they handle the removed-vs-retained decision. Understanding those differences sets up everything that follows in the series.

BMTagger — the legacy baseline

BMTagger is an NCBI host-screening workflow that combines two sequential steps: a fast bitmask-based screening step to identify candidate human reads, followed by an SRPRISM alignment step to confirm classifications. It was the standard NCBI approach for human read removal for many years and is still used as a reference point in benchmarks precisely because of its history.

The workflow looks like this:

FASTQ input
    ↓
BMFilter (bitmask k-mer screening)
    ↓
SRPRISM (alignment confirmation)
    ↓
Text file of human read IDs

Notice the output is a list of read identifiers — not FASTQ files. An additional extraction step is needed to produce the actual retained-reads FASTQ for downstream analysis.

Database

The BMTagger run used a GRCh38.p12 database consisting of two pre-built index files:

  • A bitmask (.bitmask) — used by the fast k-mer screening step
  • An SRPRISM index (.srprism.*) — used by the alignment confirmation step

Both must be built from the same reference FASTA before running.

Installation

BMTagger has legacy dependencies that can conflict with modern tools, so I kept it isolated in its own conda environment:

conda create -n bmtagger
conda activate bmtagger
# Install BMTagger via your HPC module system or conda channel
# conda install -c bioconda bmtagger   (if available)

Keeping legacy tools in isolated environments is good hygiene regardless of whether you are benchmarking — it prevents dependency conflicts that can subtly alter tool behavior.

One practical limitation: uncompressed input

The workflow I used expected uncompressed FASTQ files. The fastp outputs (.fastq.gz) had to be decompressed into a temporary working directory before BMTagger could run. I used pigz for parallel decompression:

pigz -dc sample_R1.fastp.fastq.gz > /tmp/sample_R1.fastq
pigz -dc sample_R2.fastp.fastq.gz > /tmp/sample_R2.fastq

This adds a step that the other tools in the benchmark do not require, and it has storage implications at scale — temporary uncompressed files for a 40M-read sample can be 10–15 GB each.

Running BMTagger

/usr/bin/time -v -o ${SAMPLE}_bmtagger.time.txt \
  bmtagger.sh \
    -b GRCh38_p12.bitmask \
    -x GRCh38_p12.srprism \
    -T ${TMP_DIR}/${SAMPLE} \
    -q 1 \
    -1 ${TMP_DIR}/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq \
    -2 ${TMP_DIR}/${SAMPLE}_R2.fastq \
    -o ${OUTDIR}/${SAMPLE}_taggedHuman.txt

The key flags:

  • -b — bitmask database
  • -x — SRPRISM index
  • -T — temporary working directory (needs enough space for intermediate files)
  • -q 1 — input is FASTQ (not FASTA)
  • -o — output prefix for the human read ID list

Extracting paired retained reads

Because BMTagger outputs a text file of read IDs rather than FASTQ files directly, a post-processing step is needed to extract the microbial reads you actually want:

# Get list of human read IDs from BMTagger output
grep -v "^#" ${OUTDIR}/${SAMPLE}_taggedHuman.txt > ${SAMPLE}_human_ids.txt

# Use seqtk to extract non-human reads (those NOT in the human ID list)
seqtk subseq ${TMP_DIR}/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq \
    <(grep -Fxvf ${SAMPLE}_human_ids.txt <(grep "^@" ${TMP_DIR}/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq | sed 's/^@//')) \
    > ${OUTDIR}/${SAMPLE}_bmtagger_nonhuman_R1.fastq

# Compress output
gzip ${OUTDIR}/${SAMPLE}_bmtagger_nonhuman_R1.fastq

This extraction step adds workflow complexity that Bowtie2 avoids entirely.

Bowtie2 — the modern alignment baseline

Bowtie2 uses an FM-index for fast short-read alignment and is one of the most widely used aligners in metagenomics preprocessing. For host removal, the logic is straightforward:

Paired FASTQ
    ↓
Align to human genome (GRCh38)
    ↓
Concordantly aligned pairs  →  human (discard)
Unaligned pairs             →  retain for microbiome analysis

One significant workflow advantage: Bowtie2 writes both human and non-human reads directly to FASTQ output in a single command, with no post-processing extraction step needed.

Building the reference index

bowtie2-build \
    GRCh38.fa \
    GRCh38_bowtie2_index \
    --threads 16

This step is slow (30–60 minutes for the full human genome) but only needs to be done once. Store the index in a shared location on the cluster so the same index is used for every sample.

Running Bowtie2

/usr/bin/time -v -o ${SAMPLE}_bowtie2.time.txt \
  bowtie2 \
    --very-sensitive \
    --threads 16 \
    -x ${BOWTIE2_INDEX}/GRCh38 \
    -1 ${SAMPLE}_R1.fastp.fastq.gz \
    -2 ${SAMPLE}_R2.fastp.fastq.gz \
    --un-conc-gz ${OUTDIR}/${SAMPLE}_nonhuman_R%.fastq.gz \
    --al-conc-gz ${OUTDIR}/${SAMPLE}_human_R%.fastq.gz \
    --met-file ${OUTDIR}/${SAMPLE}_bowtie2_metrics.txt \
    -S /dev/null

Key flags worth explaining:

  • --very-sensitive — uses the highest-sensitivity preset (-D 20 -R 3 -N 1 -L 20 -i S,1,0.50). For host removal, sensitivity matters more than speed — you want to find all the human reads, not just the easy ones
  • --un-conc-gz — writes both reads of pairs that did NOT align concordantly to the human genome. The % is replaced by 1 and 2 for R1 and R2. These are your retained microbial reads
  • --al-conc-gz — writes both reads of pairs that DID align concordantly. These are your human reads
  • -S /dev/null — discards the SAM alignment output (we do not need it, and it would be enormous)
  • --met-file — alignment metrics per sample, useful for QC

The --un-conc-gz and --al-conc-gz flags are the feature that makes Bowtie2 especially clean to work with for this purpose. No post-processing required — two output files per read, gzip-compressed, paired-end aware.

Side-by-side workflow comparison

Feature BMTagger Bowtie2
Input format Uncompressed FASTQ (in this workflow) Gzipped FASTQ directly
Human reference GRCh38.p12 (bitmask + SRPRISM) GRCh38 (FM-index)
Output format Text file of human read IDs Human + non-human FASTQ directly
Paired-end handling Supported Supported, explicit --un-conc-gz
Post-processing needed Yes (extract retained reads) No
Workflow complexity Higher Lower
Maintenance status Legacy Actively maintained
Role in this benchmark Historical conservative baseline Conventional modern alignment baseline

Benchmark results

Across all five samples:

Sample BMTagger removed Bowtie2 removed
Sample 1 94.88% 89.76%
Sample 2 97.91% 94.82%
Sample 3 22.51% 21.72%
Sample 4 10.52% 10.14%
Sample 5 86.07% 83.71%
Mean 62.38% 60.03%

BMTagger consistently removed a higher percentage of reads than Bowtie2 across all five samples. The difference ranges from less than one percentage point (Sample 4, low host content) to over three percentage points (Samples 1 and 2, very high host content).

The range of removal rates across samples is striking and reflects what was described on Day 1: host content varies enormously between individuals and sampling events. Sample 4 had only ~10% host reads; Samples 1 and 2 had ~90–98%. A method that performs well across this entire range is more broadly useful than one that is optimized for a narrow host-content regime.

What the removal percentages cannot tell you

BMTagger removed more reads. But this does not automatically mean BMTagger is more accurate. Those additional removed reads represent one of two possibilities:

  1. True human reads that Bowtie2 missed — in which case BMTagger is more sensitive and its additional removals are correct
  2. Microbial reads incorrectly classified as human by BMTagger — in which case its higher removal rate is actually a false-positive problem

Distinguishing between these two cases requires read-level discordance analysis, which comes on Day 5. For now, the removal rates establish the quantitative gap between methods and confirm that the two tools make different decisions — something worth investigating.

Computational performance

Approximate mean performance across the five samples:

Tool Mean wall-clock runtime Approximate peak RAM
BMTagger ~73 minutes ~8 GB
Bowtie2 ~51 minutes ~4 GB

Bowtie2 was approximately 30% faster and used roughly half the RAM of BMTagger. At scale — hundreds of samples, limited cluster allocation — this difference accumulates quickly. 25 additional CPU-hours across 20 samples is a meaningful budget difference.

These numbers were captured using the /usr/bin/time -v wrapper on every job:

/usr/bin/time -v -o ${SAMPLE}_${TOOL}.time.txt \
    tool_command ...

The verbose output includes:

Elapsed (wall clock) time:       1:13:12.48
Maximum resident set size:       8,124,456 KB
User time (seconds):             1847.23
System time (seconds):           12.41
Percent of CPU this job got:     42%

The CPU percentage is also informative. BMTagger’s 42% utilization on a 16-thread node suggests it is not parallelizing efficiently across all available cores — something to keep in mind when allocating cluster resources.

What Day 2 established

Two alignment-oriented tools using the same broad human reference can produce noticeably different removal rates. On very high-host samples (Samples 1 and 2), the gap between BMTagger and Bowtie2 is 3–5 percentage points. That translates to millions of read pairs in absolute terms on 40M-read libraries.

The operational lesson is equally clear: workflow simplicity is not trivial. BMTagger requires decompressed input, produces a read-ID list rather than FASTQ output, and needs post-processing extraction. Bowtie2 reads gzipped files directly, writes both output streams in a single command, and integrates cleanly into a modern pipeline. At scale, these differences matter for the time you spend writing and debugging pipeline code, not just the time the tool itself takes to run.

Both tools established the baseline range against which the more modern approaches — BBMap and Cleanifier — will be evaluated tomorrow.

What comes tomorrow

Day 3 covers BBMap, with a specific focus on a question that this comparison naturally raises: if two tools using the same reference can produce different results, what happens when the same tool is run against two different human references?

BBMap will be run twice — once against the standard GRCh38 and once against a repeat-masked hg19 reference. The comparison isolates the reference effect from the algorithm effect and reveals something that is easy to overlook when benchmarking host-removal tools.

Day 1 of this series is here. Day 3 publishes soon.
entry.summary: Day 2 of the host-read removal benchmark series. Today: two conventional alignment-oriented approaches — BMTagger (a legacy NCBI screening workflow) and Bowtie2 (the modern FM-index aligner). Both use GRCh38 as the human reference, both handle paired-end reads, but their workflows, computational behavior, and removal rates differ in ways that matter for high-host-content vaginal metagenomes. Includes full installation and command walkthroughs, the benchmark results across five samples, runtime and RAM comparison, and the key question the numbers alone cannot answer.

entry.title: Human Contamination Removal in Host-Associated Metagenomics: Why It Matters — Day 1 of 5

link.title: Human Contamination Removal in Host-Associated Metagenomics: Why It Matters — Day 1 of 5

entry.content:
🧬 Day 1 of 5 — Benchmarking Host-Read Removal for High-Host-Content Metagenomes

Shotgun metagenomics gives us access to microbial genomes, functional pathways, strain-level variation, and the full metabolic potential of a community — things that amplicon sequencing cannot reach. But in host-associated samples, one practical problem appears before almost any of that biology can begin: a substantial fraction of your sequencing reads may come from the host rather than the microbiome.

This is not a minor calibration issue. In some vaginal swab datasets, host-derived reads can account for the majority of the library. Process them without removing host reads first, and every downstream step — taxonomic profiling, differential abundance, functional annotation — is working with a contaminated input. Worse, the contamination is not random noise; it is a structured signal from a specific organism (you), which can create systematic artifacts in community profiles.

The standard solution is to run a host-removal step before anything else. Map your reads to the human reference genome, discard the matches, keep the rest. Simple in principle. But the question of which tool to use, with which reference, evaluated against which criteria — that is less simple than it sounds, and the choices have real consequences for the biology you ultimately report.

This post opens a five-day benchmarking series. Over the week I will run five host-removal strategies on five vaginal metagenomes, measure what each tool removes, what it retains, how fast it runs, how much memory it needs, and — most importantly — whether the reads it discards are actually human or microbial. Today is the framing: why this benchmark exists, what it measures, and what a rigorous host-removal evaluation actually needs to look at.

The two ways a host-removal tool can fail

Every host-removal method can make two types of error, and they are not symmetric in their consequences.

Error type 1: Retaining human reads. The tool misses reads that are genuinely from the host. These contaminate your microbial profile — false taxa, inflated diversity, spurious functional signals. This is the error most people think about.

Error type 2: Removing microbial reads. The tool discards reads that are genuinely from the microbiome because they share sequence similarity with the human reference. This is the error that is easy to overlook — especially when you are looking at a summary table where the fraction of incorrectly removed reads appears tiny.

The second error is the more insidious one, because its consequences are invisible in the host-removal output itself. You only see it later, downstream, when a biologically important taxon appears underrepresented or absent — and you have no easy way to know whether that is a real biological signal or an artifact of your decontamination step.

Why vaginal metagenomics is a particularly challenging case

Vaginal microbial communities are ecologically unusual. Unlike gut communities, which are highly diverse and numerically dominated by many taxa, vaginal communities can be dominated by a small number of biologically critical organisms. Depending on the individual and community state type, a sample might be overwhelmingly composed of just one or two species:

  • Lactobacillus iners — the most prevalent vaginal Lactobacillus, associated with community instability
  • Lactobacillus crispatus — associated with community stability and health
  • Gardnerella spp. — key players in bacterial vaginosis
  • Sneathia vaginalis, Fannyhessea vaginae, Aerococcus christensenii — associated with BV and adverse reproductive outcomes
  • Metamycoplasma hominis — a common BV-associated organism with an unusual genome

This low-diversity, high-dominance structure means that if a host-removal tool systematically discards reads from even one of these taxa — because those reads share a short region of sequence similarity with the human genome — the biological impact is disproportionately large. The overall false-positive removal rate in your summary statistics might be 0.1%. The impact on your L. iners abundance estimate might be 15%.

The question is therefore not simply “which tool removes the most reads?” A more precise question is:

Which method provides the best balance between human-read removal sensitivity, microbial-read specificity, runtime, memory use, and workflow reproducibility — at the sample-level host content typical of vaginal specimens?

The benchmark design

Five paired-end vaginal metagenomes were selected to span a broad range of host contamination levels. All sample identifiers are anonymized for this public technical series.

Sample Input read pairs Host content category
Sample 1 41,644,670 Very high
Sample 2 43,344,280 Very high
Sample 3 41,089,173 Moderate
Sample 4 31,349,380 Low
Sample 5 37,060,999 High
Total 194,488,502 —

The range matters. A tool that performs well on a low-host sample might struggle on a very high-host sample, or vice versa. Evaluating across this range gives a more honest picture of how each method scales with the biological reality of the input.

Standardizing the input: fastp first

Before any host-removal tool saw the data, all samples were processed with fastp — quality trimming, adapter removal, quality filtering. Every host-removal method then received exactly the same quality-controlled reads.

This step is non-negotiable for a fair comparison. If method A receives raw reads and method B receives trimmed reads, you are measuring two different things simultaneously and cannot attribute differences in outcome to the host-removal algorithm. Standardizing input is the first rule of tool benchmarking.

fastp \
  --in1 sample_R1.fastq.gz \
  --in2 sample_R2.fastq.gz \
  --out1 sample_fastp_R1.fastq.gz \
  --out2 sample_fastp_R2.fastq.gz \
  --json sample_fastp.json \
  --html sample_fastp.html \
  --thread 8 \
  --detect_adapter_for_pe \
  --qualified_quality_phred 20 \
  --length_required 50

The five methods being compared

Method Strategy Why it is included
BMTagger Legacy k-mer screening + alignment Historical baseline; still used in some lab workflows
Bowtie2 FM-index alignment to GRCh38 Widely used conventional approach
BBMap + GRCh38 k-mer-seeded hybrid mapping Flexible, high-sensitivity mapper against standard reference
BBMap + masked hg19 Hybrid mapping to repeat-masked reference Tests whether reference masking changes removal rates
Cleanifier Modern probabilistic filtering, pangenome-aware Very fast; designed for clinical and high-host-content samples

One thing that became clear immediately while planning this benchmark: the reference genome can matter almost as much as the aligner. BBMap run against GRCh38 is not the same as BBMap run against a repeat-masked hg19 reference. The algorithm is identical; the database is different. Both comparisons belong in a rigorous evaluation, which is why BBMap appears twice.

This means the benchmark is measuring two things simultaneously:

  1. Algorithm effects — does the underlying alignment or classification strategy matter?
  2. Reference effects — does the choice of human reference change what gets removed?

What the benchmark measures

A single “percentage of reads removed” number is not enough. For each tool on each sample, I tracked:

Metric Why it matters
% read pairs classified as human Primary removal rate
Retained non-human read pairs What goes into downstream analysis
Wall-clock runtime Practical compute cost
Peak RAM (maximum resident set size) Determines whether tool runs on a laptop vs HPC
CPU usage Efficiency of parallelization
Discordant pairs between methods Reads that one tool removes but another retains — the scientifically interesting subset
Evidence of microbial false-positive removal Whether any known vaginal taxa are being incorrectly discarded

The last two metrics require extra work beyond running the tool — they require cross-comparing outputs and mapping retained/discarded reads back to taxonomic assignments. But they are the metrics that actually answer the biological question.

Measuring compute cost with /usr/bin/time -v

Every tool run was wrapped with:

/usr/bin/time -v tool_command \
  2> sample_tool_timing.txt

The -v flag (verbose mode) reports:

Elapsed (wall clock) time:    0:04:23.15
Maximum resident set size:    12,847,316 KB
User time (seconds):          187.34
System time (seconds):        6.21
Percent of CPU this job got:  73%

This is more informative than timing alone — it tells you whether the tool is memory-bound (relevant for deciding whether it can run on a standard server or requires HPC), and whether it parallelizes efficiently (relevant for estimating how long it will take at scale).

HPC infrastructure: SLURM array jobs

Benchmarking full metagenomes on a laptop is impractical. The full workflow ran on an HPC cluster organized as a SLURM array:

5 samples × 5 tool configurations = 25 benchmark jobs

Each job received the same fastp-preprocessed inputs, wrote tool-specific outputs to a structured directory, and generated three additional files per run: a timing file, a command record, and a status file.

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=host_removal_benchmark
#SBATCH --array=1-25
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/benchmark_%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/benchmark_%A_%a.err

# Each array task reads its sample and tool assignment from a lookup table
SAMPLE=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" benchmark_jobs.txt | awk '{print $1}')
TOOL=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" benchmark_jobs.txt | awk '{print $2}')

# Tool-specific commands are dispatched from here
bash run_${TOOL}.sh ${SAMPLE}

The benchmark_jobs.txt file is a 25-line table mapping array task IDs to sample-tool combinations. This design makes the benchmark fully auditable: every job’s exact command, input, and output is recorded, and any individual job can be rerun in isolation if needed.

The full workflow

Raw paired-end FASTQ
        ↓
fastp preprocessing (same for all methods)
        ↓
Standardized quality-controlled input
        ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│  5 host-removal tools in parallel │
│  BMTagger                         │
│  Bowtie2 → GRCh38                │
│  BBMap → GRCh38                  │
│  BBMap → masked hg19             │
│  Cleanifier                       │
└──────────────┬───────────────────┘
               ↓
   Human reads (discarded) + Retained reads
               ↓
   Runtime / RAM / removal rate per tool
               ↓
   Read-level discordance analysis
   (which reads does only one tool remove?)
               ↓
   Microbial specificity validation
   (are any vaginal taxa being falsely removed?)
               ↓
   Final comparison table

The last two steps — discordance analysis and microbial specificity validation — are the ones that distinguish a benchmark from simply running five tools and comparing numbers. Two methods can remove nearly identical percentages of reads while disagreeing substantially on which specific reads those are. If the disagreement is concentrated in reads from Gardnerella or L. iners, the two methods are not equivalent even if their removal rates look the same.

What comes next

Over the next four days:

Day 2 — BMTagger and Bowtie2: installation, reference preparation, paired-end commands, outputs, and why BMTagger remains a useful baseline despite being much slower than modern alternatives.

Day 3 — BBMap with GRCh38 and masked hg19: how to run BBMap for host removal, what the reference masking actually changes, and first results from the high-host samples.

Day 4 — Cleanifier: the newest method in the benchmark, designed specifically for high-host-content clinical metagenomes, with a pangenome-aware approach that differs substantially from the alignment-based tools.

Day 5 — Full comparison: all five methods side by side. Removal rates, runtime, RAM, discordant read analysis, and which tool performs best across the range of host content represented in these samples.

The central principle of this benchmark

The metric I am optimizing for is not maximum human-read removal. A tool that removes 99.9% of human reads while also removing 5% of Lactobacillus reads is not a better tool — it is a differently failing tool, in a way that is harder to detect and more damaging to biological interpretation.

The metric that actually matters is closer to:

High host-removal sensitivity
      +
High microbial-read specificity
      +
Reasonable compute cost
      +
Reproducible, auditable workflow

Whether any single tool achieves all four is what this benchmark will determine.

Sample identifiers have been anonymized for this public technical series. The benchmark is presented to illustrate workflow design and method comparison. Day 2 publishes soon.
entry.summary: Shotgun metagenomics of host-associated samples has a problem that appears before any biology can begin: a large fraction of your reads may come from the host, not the microbiome. In vaginal samples, cervical swabs, saliva, skin, or nasal specimens, host-derived reads can dominate the library. The standard advice is to remove them — but the question of which tool to use, with which reference, and how to measure whether you are doing it correctly, is less straightforward than it appears. This post opens a 5-day benchmarking series comparing BMTagger, Bowtie2, BBMap (GRCh38 and masked hg19), and Cleanifier on five vaginal metagenomes spanning a broad range of host contamination.
